κεχωλωμένοις τὰς βάσεις, τῆς ψυχῆς πόδας· καὶ τῷ λόγῳ ἐγίνετο αὐτὸς αὐτῶν ποῦς.
Στίχ. ι ʹ. ∆ίκην δὲ ἣν οὐκ ᾔδειν, ἐξιχνίασα. ∆ιδάσκει ἡμᾶς πῶς δεῖ δικάζειν, ἐάν ποτε
κλη θῶμεν ἐπὶ δίαιταν ἀδελφῶν, ὥστε διαιτῆσαι τὰ κατ' αὐτούς. ΚΕΦ. ΛΒʹ. Στίχ. αʹ.
Καὶ ἐπαύσατο Ἰὼβ ῥήμασιν. Ἡσύχασαν δὲ καὶ οἱ τρεῖς φίλοι αὐτοῦ ἔτι ἀντειπεῖν Ἰώβ.
Ἦν γὰρ Ἰὼβ δίκαιος ἐναντίον αὐτῶν. Οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἐπαύσατο. Καρδία δὲ ἦν αὐτοῦ
νοοῦσα τὰ θεῖα, οὐκ ἐπαύσατο. Ἤδη γὰρ καιρὸς τῷ παντὶ πράγματι ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανὸν,
καιρὸς τοῦ σιγᾷν καὶ καιρὸς τοῦ λαλεῖν. Ὅτε οὖν καιρὸς τοῦ ἀποκρίνασθαι πρὸς τοὺς
τρεῖς, ἔλεγεν· ὅτε ἦν καιρὸς, μετὰ τὸ ἐπι στομίσαι αὐτοὺς, ἐσίγησε. Καὶ οἶμαι ἐν
ἐπαίνῳ λέ γεσθαι τὸ, Ἐπαύσατο ὁ Ἰώβ. Στίχ. ζʹ. ∆ιὸ ἡσύχασα, φοβηθεὶς τοῦ ὑμῖν ἀναγ
γεῖλαι τὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ἐπιστήμην. Ἐπιστήμην ἔχει, πῶς ἄνθρωποι πάσχουσι· διὰ τί
ἄνθρωποι ἐν περιστάσεσί τισιν ἐν τῷ βίῳ τούτῳ μόνῳ γίνονται· ὅσοι ἄδικοι ὄντες
εὐτυχοῦσιν. Εἶδον ἀδι κοῦντας καὶ παρανομοῦντας, καὶ ἐμοῦ παρὰ μι κρὸν
ἐσαλεύθησαν οἱ πόδες. Ἐὰν ἐν τῷ βίῳ τούτῳ μόνον ἐνίδω, παρ' ὀλίγον ἐξεχύθη τὰ
διαβήματά μου. Στίχ. ιʹ. Οὐχ οἱ πολυχρόνιοί εἰσι σοφοί. Οὐ γὰρ ἀνάγκη, φησὶ, τοὺς
πρεσβύτας μόνους εἶναι σοφούς· ἀλλ' ἔστι καὶ ἀπὸ νεότητος ἀκοῦσαί τι γενναῖον. Εἰ
γὰρ χρόνος ποιεῖ σοφοὺς, πολλῷ μᾶλλον Θεός. Στίχ. ιηʹ. Ὠλέκει γάρ με τὸ πνεῦμα
τῆς γαστρός. Ὥσπερ τις ἔγκυος γίνεται, καὶ μορφωθέντος τοῦ γεννωμένου ἐν αὐτῷ,
ἐπὶ ὠδῖνας ἔρχεται, μέχρις οὗ ἀπογεννήσῃ τοῦτο ὃ πρότερον συνείληφε· τοιοῦ τόν τί
μοι νόει γενέσθαι καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ φιλομα θοῦς ψυχῆς. Συλλαμβάνει γὰρ τὸν λόγον
ὃν ἀπαγγελ λόμενον μορφοῖ καὶ τυποῖ αὐτὸν τῇ τάξει. Ὅτ' ἂν δὲ μετὰ τὸ τυπῶσαι
καὶ μορφῶσαι αὐτὸν ἕτοιμον γενόμε νον, μὴ ὡς ἔκτρωμα ἀνέτοιμον καὶ ἀτελὲς

γαστήρ μου ὥσπερ ἀσκὸς γλεύκους ζέων δεδεμένος. ∆οκεῖ μοι ἐντεῦθεν εἰρῆσθαι τὸ
ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ. 17.96 Οὐδεὶς οἶνον νέον εἰς ἀσκοὺς παλαιοὺς βάλλει Στίχ. κʹ.
Λαλήσω, ἵνα ἀναπαύσωμαι ἀνοίξας τὰ χείλη. Ὁ τυγχάνων συνετοῦ ἀκροατοῦ, καὶ

Οὐκ ἔχω ταύτην τὴν ἐπιστήμην, ἵνα θαυμάσω πρόσωπον· ἀλλὰ καταφρονῶ
ἀνθρώπων, καὶ τῆς παρ' αὐτοῖς αἰ σχύνης βροτῶν, καὶ τῆς παρ' αὐτοῖς ἐντροπῆς.
Στίχ. κβʹ. Εἰ δὲ μὴ, καὶ ἐμὲ σῆτες ἔδονται. Ὡς τῶν σητῶν διεσθιόντων τοὺς
λαμβάνοντας πρόσ ωπα ἀνθρώπων. ΚΕΦ. ΛΕʹ. Στίχ. ʹ. Εἰ ἥμαρτες, τί πράξεις; Ἐὰν
ἀναβλέψῃς εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν, καὶ κατανοήσῃς τὰ νέφη, νοήσεις τί ἥμαρτες. Τί σε
πρᾶξαι δεῖ; Προσέρχεσθαι τῷ ἀρχιερεῖ, καὶ παρακαλεῖν, ἵνα ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς προσαγάγῃ
θυσίαν περὶ σοῦ. Ἐὰν γάρ τις ἁμάρτῃ, παράκλητον ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα Ἰησοῦν
Χριστὸν δίκαιον, καὶ αὐτὸς ἱλασμός ἐστι περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων ἡμῶν. Στίχ. ʹ. Εἰ δὲ
καὶ πολλὰ ἠνόμησας, τί δύνασαι ποιῆσαι; Τὸ τηλικοῦτον ποιήσεις· ἀναλύσεις σου τὰς
πολλὰς ἀνομίας. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀνιάτοις, οἷς ἑαυ τοὺς ἰάσασθαι οὐ δυνάμεθα,
ἦλθεν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ἐξ οὐρανῶν, ἵνα τὰ ἀνίατα ἰάσηται, καὶ γίνηται τό· Μακάριοι,
ὧν ἀφέθησαν αἱ ἀνομίαι, καὶ ὧν ἀπε καλύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι. Στίχ. ζʹ. Ἐπειδὴ οὖν
δίκαιος εἶ, τί δώσεις αὐτῷ; Ἀλλ' εἰ δίκαιος εἶ ὡς πρὸς Θεὸν, τί ἔχεις δοῦναι κατὰ τὴν
σὴν δικαιοσύνην; Εἰ δὲ καὶ ὡς λέγεις δίκαιος εἶ, τί προσθήσεις αὐτῷ; Στίχ. ιʹ. Ὁ
κατατάσσων φυλακὰς νυκτερινάς. Ἐγκώμια τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ αἴνους καὶ ὕμνους αὐτοῦ
διεξέρχεται. Ὁ κατατάσσων φυλακὰς νυκτε ρινὰς, αὐτὸς ὁ Θεός ἐστι. Θέλω ἰδεῖν,
πῶς κατατάσσων ἐστὶν ὁ Θεὸς φυ λακὰς νυκτερινάς. Ὅλως ὁ αἰὼν οὗτος νύξ ἐστι,
σκό τος ἐστί. Τὸ φῶς τηρεῖταί σοι. Ὃ βλέπεις νῦν φῶς, δι' ἐσόπτρου βλέπεις· Καὶ ἐν
τῷ φωτί σου ὀψόμεθα φῶς. Μέλλομέν ποτε βλέπειν αὐτό. Οὐκοῦν νύξ ἐστι πᾶς ὁ
αἰών· ἐπεὶ νύξ ἐστι, πόλεμοι πολλοὶ, πολ λὰ θηρία περιέρχεται. Στίχ. ιαʹ. Ὁ διορίζων
με ἀπὸ τετραπόδων γῆς. Ἐὰν ᾖς ἁμαρτωλὸς, οὐ διωρίσθης ἀπὸ τῶν τετραπόδων γῆς.
Ἄνθρωπος γὰρ ἐν τιμῇ ὢν, οὐ συνῆκε. Παρασυνεβλήθη τοῖς κτήνεσι τοῖς ἀνοή τοις,
καὶ ὡμοιώθη αὐτοῖς. Ἐὰν ᾖς ἁμαρτωλὸς, οὐ διωρίσθης ἀπὸ τῶν τετραπόδων τῆς γῆς·
ἀλλὰ λέγε ταί σοι· Μὴ γίνεσθε ὡς ἵππος καὶ ἡμίονος, οἷς οὐκ 17.97 ἔστι σύνεσις. –Καὶ
pass_a_gloss: …saying (letter), as much power as there is, we ought to help the poor, oppressed by the powerful. Verse 15. And a foot to a lame one. He himself was granting also to those lamed the steps, feet of the soul; and by the word he himself became their foot. Verse 16 (numeral damaged). And a cause which I did not know, I tracked out. He teaches us how one must judge, if ever we are called upon an arbitration of brothers, so as to arbitrate the things about them. Chapter 32, verse 1. And Job ceased in words. And his three friends also were quiet still to speak against Job. For Job was righteous before them. Not simply did he cease. But his heart, understanding the divine things, did not cease. For already there is a time for every matter under heaven, a time of being silent and a time of speaking. When then it was a time of answering toward the three, he was speaking; when it was the time, after stopping their mouths, he was silent. And I think the 'Job ceased' is said in praise. Verse 6 (labelled 7). Therefore I was quiet, having feared to announce to you my own knowledge. He has knowledge how men suffer; why men come to be in certain circumstances in this life alone; as many as being unjust prosper. I saw people doing injustice and transgressing the law, and of me by a little my feet were shaken. If in this life alone I look, by a little my steps were poured out. Verse 9 (labelled 10). Not the long-timed are wise. For it is not necessary, he says, for the elders alone to be wise; but it is possible also from youth to hear something noble. For if time makes wise, much more God. Verse 18. For the spirit of the belly destroys me. Just as someone becomes pregnant, and when the thing being born in her has been formed, she comes upon birth-pangs, until she gives birth to this which she conceived before; think for me something such to happen also upon the soul of the learning-lover. For it conceives the word, which being announced it forms and stamps it in order. And whenever after stamping and forming it having become ready, it hands it over not as an unready and incomplete miscarriage, but as brought to term and completed, I would say. Verse 19. And my belly like a wineskin of must boiling, bound. It seems to me from here to have been said the thing in the Gospel: No one puts new wine into old wineskins. Verse 20. I will speak, so that I may rest, having opened the lips. The one meeting an understanding hearer, and being full of words, speaking rests, and says: I will speak, so that I may rest. Verse 22 (label as printed; KJV 32:21-22). For I do not know how to admire a face. For I do not know how to admire a face (the lemma is printed twice). I do not have this knowledge, so that I admire a face; but I despise men, and the shame of mortals among them, and the regard among them. Verse 22. But if not, moths will eat me also. As the moths devouring those receiving faces of men. Chapter 35, verse 6 (numeral lost). If you sinned, what will you do? If you look up to the heaven and consider the clouds, you will understand what you sinned. What must you do? Come to the high priest, and beseech, so that the high priest may bring a sacrifice about you. For if someone sins, we have an advocate toward the Father, Jesus Christ righteous, and he is propitiation about our sins. Verse 6 (numeral lost). And if also you did many lawless things, what can you do? You will do such a great thing: you will dissolve your many lawlessnesses. Because of this, upon the incurable things, which we cannot heal ourselves, Jesus Christ came from the heavens, so that he might heal the incurable things, and there might come to be the: Blessed are they whose lawlessnesses were forgiven, and whose sins were covered. Verse 7. Since then you are righteous, what will you give him? But if you are righteous as toward God, what do you have to give according to your righteousness? And if also as you say you are righteous, what will you add to him? Verse 10. The one arranging night watches. He goes through encomia of God, and praises and his hymns. The one arranging night watches, he himself is God. I want to see how God is arranging night watches. Wholly this age is night, it is darkness. The light is kept for you. What light you now see, through a mirror you see; and in your light we shall see light. We are going sometime to see it. Therefore the whole age is night; since it is night, many wars, many beasts go about. Verse 11. The one separating me from four-footed beasts of earth. If you are a sinner, you were not separated from the four-footed beasts of earth. For a man being in honour did not understand. He was compared to the senseless cattle, and was made like them. If you are a sinner, you were not separated from the four-footed of the earth; but it is said to you: Do not become as horse and mule, which have no understanding. And…
pass_b_english: … letter, we ought, as far as our strength allows, to help the poor who are oppressed by the powerful.
“And a foot to the lame” (Job 29:15). He himself gave steps even to those who were lamed, feet for the soul; and by his word he himself became their foot.
“And a cause I did not know, I searched out” (Job 29:16). He teaches us how we ought to judge, if we are ever called to arbitrate between brothers, so as to settle their affairs.

“And Job ceased from his words” (Job 31:40). “And his three friends also held their peace and no longer answered Job, for Job was righteous before them” (Job 32:1). He did not simply cease. His heart, which understood divine things, did not cease. For there is a time for every matter under heaven (Ecclesiastes 3:1): “a time to keep silent and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). So when it was the time to answer the three, he spoke; when it was the time, after he had stopped their mouths, he fell silent. And I think the words “Job ceased” are said in his praise.

“Therefore I held my peace, afraid to declare my own knowledge to you” (Job 32:6). He has knowledge of how human beings suffer, of why human beings fall into certain straits if one looks at this life alone, and of how many prosper though they are unjust. I saw people doing wrong and breaking the law, and my feet were almost shaken. If I look into this life alone, my steps were all but poured away (Psalm 73:2).

“It is not the long-lived who are wise” (Job 32:9). For it does not follow, he says, that only old men are wise; it is possible to hear something noble from youth too. For if time makes people wise, God does so much more.

“For the spirit of my belly is destroying me” (Job 32:18). Just as a woman becomes pregnant, and when the child being born in her has been formed, she comes to her labor pains until she gives birth to what she had conceived before: think with me that something of this kind happens in the soul of the one who loves learning too. It conceives the word, and as it is being declared it shapes it and stamps it with order. And when, after stamping and shaping it, the word has become ready, it hands it over not as an unready and unfinished miscarriage, but, I would say, as something brought to term and made complete.

“And my belly is like a skin of new wine, fermenting and tied up” (Job 32:19). It seems to me that the saying in the Gospel was spoken from this place: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins” (Mark 2:22).

“I will speak so that I may find rest, when I have opened my lips” (Job 32:20). A man who meets with an understanding hearer, and is full of words, finds rest in speaking, and says: “I will speak so that I may find rest.”

“For I do not know how to admire a face” (Job 32:22). I do not have this skill, of admiring a person's face. No, I despise human beings, and the shame that mortals can bring, and the respect that they command.
“Otherwise the moths will devour me too” (Job 32:22). As though the moths eat through those who show partiality to the faces of men.

“If you have sinned, what will you do?” (Job 35:6). If you look up to heaven and consider the clouds, you will understand how you have sinned. What must you do? Come to the high priest and beg the high priest to offer a sacrifice for you. For “if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1-2).

“And if you have done much lawlessness, what can you do?” (Job 35:6). You will do this great thing: you will undo your many lawless deeds. That is why, for the incurable ills that we cannot heal in ourselves, Jesus Christ came from heaven, so that he might heal what is incurable and the word might come true: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 32:1).

“Well then, since you are righteous, what will you give him?” (Job 35:7). But if you are righteous before God, what do you have to give in keeping with your righteousness? And if you are righteous, as you say, what will you add to him?

“He who appoints the night watches” (Job 35:10). He goes through the praises of God, his commendations and his hymns. The one who appoints the night watches is God himself. I want to see how God is the one who appoints the night watches. This whole age is night; it is darkness. The light is being kept for you. The light you see now, you see through a mirror (1 Corinthians 13:12). And “in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 36:9): one day we are going to see it. So the whole age is night; and since it is night, there are many wars, and many wild beasts prowl about.

“He who separates me from the four-footed beasts of the earth” (Job 35:11). If you are a sinner, you have not been separated from the four-footed beasts of the earth. For “man, being in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless cattle and became like them” (Psalm 49:20). If you are a sinner, you have not been separated from the four-footed beasts of the earth; rather, it is said to you: “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 32:9). And …

choices.choice: Δοκεῖ μοι ἐντεῦθεν εἰρῆσθαι rendered first person: 'It seems to me that the saying in the Gospel was spoken from this place'. Also 'I think' (οἶμαι) and 'think with me' (μοι νόει) kept.
'Chapter 32:', 'Chapter 35:' and 'Elihu:' removed; references only after lemmas.

Ἐμοῦ παρὰ μικρὸν ἐσαλεύθησαν οἱ πόδες / παρ' ὀλίγον ἐξεχύθη τὰ διαβήματά μου is LXX Psalm 72:2, cited once as Psalm 73:2; the commentator's sentence frame ('I saw people doing wrong', 'If I look into this life alone') kept.
The Greek prints 'Οὐ γὰρ ἐπίσταμαι θαυμάσαι πρόσωπον' twice; translated once, recorded.
